content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new neural network-based method to perform sorting of abstract inputs such as multi-digit images by use of permutation-equivariant transformers and “error-free differentiable swap functions”. In order to achieve this, they first define a relaxation gap between the usual nonsmooth max/min swap function vs a smooth relaxation via a sigmoid function. This gap can be large if swap functions are applied numerous times in the sorting network. The authors then propose an error-free swap function that, in a forward pass, uses the usual max/min swap function, and in a backward pass during gradient computation, uses the sigmoid relaxation. Finally, the authors propose a new methodology to sort multi-digit images by first finding a permutation-equivariant representation using a transformer without positional encoding, before feeding said representation to the sorting network. This pipeline can be trained end-to-end with an appropriate loss function. Experiments are conducted on usual benchmark datasets such as MNIST and SVHN to verify the claims.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1. The proposed usage of permutation-equivariant transformers is interesting and backed by vast literature of the benefit of incorporating symmetries into the architecture/training process.
2. The implementation as a whole is relatively simple and prompts interesting new directions in utilizing symmetries in neural sorting algorithms.
3. Experimental results are strong and consistently outperform other methods with similar FLOPs and number of parameters. 
4. The highlighted issue of error accumulation is relevant when scaling the number of swap functions in the sorting network. (Figure 1)

Weaknesses
1. The paper would benefit from more detailed comparison to existing works (Section 6 Related work is simply listing other works without a clear comparison).  
2. Proposition 1 is rather trivial and does not seem to be used anywhere else in the paper. The proof of this proposition in the appendix is also a paraphrase of the first part of Lemma 3, Petersen et al. 2022 proof. 
3. The proposed error-free differentiable swap function is more of an implementation detail to prevent smooth relaxation of swap functions from modifying the inputs; rather than an actual differentiable function (as opposed to prior work) in a mathematical sense. In fact, the proposal is equivalent to redefining the (sub)derivative of the non-differentiable max/min function as that of a sigmoid function. While the same idea was used in straight-through estimator in Bengio et al. 2013, the fact that such an estimator is usually biased is undesirable.   
4. As a result, the theory and justification behind these engineering details are not the strongest possible. 

Additional remarks
1. In the explanation of equation 4, the authors claimed that ‘Without loss of generality, we can express min and max … where … sigma(.) in [0,1] transforms an input to bounded value, i.e., a probability over the input.’ The necessary property for \sigma to work in such a formulation is that \sigma(x) > 0.5 iff x > 0; on top of having bounded value in [0,1] (i.e, there exists \sigma having value in [0,1] but cannot be used to make the min/max formulation correct). I suggest simply defining the \sigma function as a sigmoid function in the explanation of equation 4 instead of doing so in equation 5. 
2. In equation 14, and in the proof of Proposition 1 in the appendix, the matrix P seems to take non-integral values (output of a sigmoid function), which is not clearly stated in the main text, section 2 when it was first introduced. This is slightly misleading since the authors referred to P as a permutation matrix (which by definition has only 0,1 entries). I suggest making the construction of P_i more clearly in the main text Section 2 and refer to it as a ‘relaxed permutation matrix’ (as was done in Petersen et al. 2022)
3. Figure 1 and 2 legends and axis labels are barely visible in print, but contain very important information. The dash vs continuous plot in figure one are also barely different in print. I suggest increasing the size of the plot and/or the font size of the labels.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Clarity:
a. The paper can highlight more clearly what are the novel ideas that the paper brings (for example, Is this the first work to use a permutation-equivariant transformer in this task? If not, how is it different from previous usage.)  
b. Language used is clear apart from some small typos. 
2. Quality:
The paper was able to outperform existing methods on benchmark datasets. 
3. Novelty:
The paper contains various novel implementation and engineering details that are relevant and suggestive of new directions. However, the novelty can be more clearly highlighted in the writing.
4. Reproducibility:
The submission includes details on the neural architectures used and ablation studies, as well as the code used to run. Although I have yet to run the code myself due to lack of time and resources, I believe the results in the paper are either reproducible or can be quickly proven to be irreproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that the paper, despite being relatively simple and having weak theoretical backing and justification, presents interesting workable directions in differentiable sorting algorithms. I recommend weak acceptance, in expectation that the writing is clean up and novelty/comparison more adequately highlighted in the final version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce an improved version of the differentiable swap function from Petersen et. al.   They show that with this swap function, a sorting network gets higher accuracy on two toy datasets where the "value" of each input needs to be imputed along with the sort of a set of inputs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
   as far as I can tell, the paper is correct.  The approach is well motivated _within_ the context of the problem of end-to-end sorting with a differentiable swap function.

Weaknesses:
  in my opinion, the paper is not well motivated.  There is no attempt (beyond the two toys) to give a reason why a practitioner might want to use such a learned sorting method; and because of this, it is unclear whether the larger scale framing makes sense.  With this in mind, it is difficult to see the value in the authors' relatively technical contribution.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:  the text itself is not well written

Novelty: within the framing of neural sorting with differentiable swaps, the authors make a technical contribution.  It is unclear to me how much this will be useful beyond this relatively narrow framing.

Quality:  the mentioned technical contribution is not negligible, but is quite specialized afaict.  In a more central problem this might be a high-quality work.

Reproducibility: good.
content.summary_of_the_review: As much as I appreciate careful technical work, I find the framing of the problem too cargo-culted from Petersen et. al. and Grover et. al.  To justify a work of this kind of narrow technical progress requires a motivating problem with real applications, or with good reasons from the literature to consider the problem important.  The data used to motivate and evaluate the approach in this paper are far too contrived to support this level of technical work. Furthermore, even on these toys, the results are not good in an absolute sense (even if they are improvements over previous approaches); neural sorting as described here does not reliably work even on smallish sequences of length a few tens.   It is thus difficult to evaluate the impact of any technical approach to the greater community.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle the sorting problem. They define a softening error by a differentiable swap function, and develop an error free swap function that holds non-decreasing and differentiability conditions. They utilize the transformer model to achieve this, which requires the supervision of the soft and hard permutation masks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The design of the error-free differentiable swap function has some novelty. They only back-propagate the gradients of approximated min and max, but in the forward propagation, they compute exactly. 
Weakness:
1. The experimental results are not exciting and do not provide enough new knowledge to the area. If the goal of this work is to teach the neural network how to sort and generalize to larger sizes, prior works have done that. For example, in [1], they also adapt the transformer model and use supervision on the attention mask. They avoid the softening error issues by using hard attention in the prediction, which is similar to yours. They maintain almost 100% accuracy even when sequence lengths reach 100. Compared to the experiments shown in Table 1 and Table 2, the results shown by this work are less interesting. Furthermore, the model proposed by this work can only do sorting while [1] also performs other algorithmic tasks. Besides, pointer network [2] is also a good baseline as they are known for generalizability to larger sizes.
2. I have doubts about the error-free claim. The gradients back propagated are not the true gradients of the forward path. How can the authors ensure that there will be no error introduced by this?

Literature:
[1] Neural execution engines: Learning to execute subroutines. Yujun Yan, Kevin Swersky, Danai Koutra, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, Milad Hashemi. NeurIPS 2020.
[2] Pointer Networks. Oriol Vinyals, Meire Fortunato, Navdeep Jaitly. NeurIPS 2015.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, the paper is clear. But the way they illustrate that their proposed method is error-free can be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: I do not support this paper mainly for two reasons: (1) their proposed models can only be applied to learn the swap function. Sorting is a solved problem and it lacks the motivation why we want to teach the neural network to do it. (2) Their proposed model does not show very good generalizability as prior works have shown.

content.title: Neural Sorting Networks with Error-Free Differentiable Swap Functions
content.abstract: Sorting is a fundamental operation of all computer systems, having been a long-standing significant research topic. Beyond the problem formulation of traditional sorting algorithms, we consider sorting problems for more abstract yet expressive inputs e.g., multi-digit images and image fragments, through a neural sorting network. To learn a mapping from a high-dimensional input to an ordinal variable, the differentiability of sorting networks needs to be guaranteed. In this paper we define a softening error by a differentiable swap function, and develop an error-free swap function that holds non-decreasing and differentiability conditions. Furthermore, a permutation-equivariant Transformer network with multi-head attention is adopted to capture dependency between given inputs and also leverage its model capacity. Experiments on diverse sorting benchmarks demonstrate that our method performs better than or comparable to existing baseline methods.
